Getting Started with stratsampling

Source: vignettes/package_overview.Rmd
package_overview.Rmd

Introduction

Many studies now use a surrogate outcome, such as a machine-coded or AI-generated score, when the outcome of interest is expensive to obtain. The surrogate may be available for every unit, but it is not the actual outcome. If the surrogate is systematically off, estimates based on it alone can also be off.

Mozer and Miratrix (2025) describe one way to use a human-coded subsample to correct this bias. The researcher codes a random subset of units, compares the human-coded outcomes to the surrogate outcomes in that subset, and uses the observed differences to adjust the full-sample surrogate estimate. Mozer, Pashley, and Miratrix (2026) extend this idea by asking which units should be selected for human coding. When surrogate errors vary across observable groups, stratified sampling can reduce uncertainty by making the human-coded sample more informative.

The workflow below has four parts:

  1. Stratification: Create and evaluate stratifications based on surrogate scores and covariates.
  2. Sample: Draw stratified samples with proportional or custom allocation across strata.
  3. Estimate: Compute model-assisted estimators that combine surrogate predictions with bias-corrected adjustments from the coded subsample.
  4. Analyze Power: Compare the precision of stratified and simple random sampling designs for different levels of coding effort.

Installation

Install the package from GitHub, then load it:

# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("lmiratrix/stratsampling")
library(stratsampling)

A complete workflow

The example uses the package’s built-in toy dataset. The workflow has five steps: load data, choose a stratification, draw a sample, merge the coded outcomes, and estimate the treatment effect.

Step 1: Load the data

Suppose you have data from an RCT with a machine-coded surrogate outcome (Yhat) for every unit. The true outcome is expensive to obtain, so it will only be observed for a human-coded subsample. The dataset also contains baseline covariates and a treatment indicator:

data( toy_data )
head( toy_data )
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>      ID    X1    X2    X3    Tx   Yhat
#>   <int> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1     1  0.85     1     2     0  1.79 
#> 2     2 -0.9      1     3     0  8.44 
#> 3     3  0.16     1     3     0 -0.531
#> 4     4  0.12     1     3     0  0.861
#> 5     5 -0.57     1     3     0 -2.69 
#> 6     6  0.19     1     3     0 -1.16

The toy_data dataset contains 1000 observations with three baseline covariates (X1, X2, X3), a surrogate prediction (Yhat), treatment assignment (Tx), and a unique identifier (ID). X3 is known to be highly predictive of the actual outcome.

Step 2: Create and evaluate candidate stratifications

The first design choice is how to stratify the population. The create_stratification_candidates() function generates candidate stratifications based on different variables and numbers of strata:

candidates <- create_stratification_candidates( toy_data,
                                                vars = c("Yhat", "X1", "X2", "X3"),
                                                Z = "Tx" )
length( candidates )
#> [1] 39

Each candidate is a factor vector assigning every observation to a stratum. To compare candidates before coding, use compare_stratifications_precoding(). This ranks the candidates using proxy metrics based only on the surrogate outcome and observed covariates:

comparison_precoding <- compare_stratifications_precoding( toy_data,
                                                           candidates,
                                                           Z = "Tx" )
head( comparison_precoding )
#> # A tibble: 6 × 9
#>   stratification   n_strata min_stratum_size max_stratum_size avg_size_ratio
#>   <chr>               <int>            <int>            <int>          <dbl>
#> 1 Yhat_quintiles          5              100              100           1   
#> 2 Yhat_quartiles          4              125              125           1   
#> 3 Yhat_X2_3xlevels       12               11               84           6.17
#> 4 Yhat_X2_3x3             9               28               99           3.17
#> 5 Yhat_X2_3x2             6               30              137           3.92
#> 6 Yhat_X3_3xlevels        9               46               63           1.33
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: mean_spread <dbl>, avg_within_var_Yhat <dbl>,
#> #   sd_within_var_Yhat <dbl>, total_var_Yhat <dbl>

The table orders candidates by these pre-coding metrics. Here, we use a 3-by-3 interaction stratification because X3 was constructed to be predictive of surrogate accuracy.

The make_interaction_strata() function creates such stratifications directly:

toy_data$strata <- make_interaction_strata( x1 = toy_data$Yhat, 
                                            n1 = 3, 
                                            var_name1 = "Yhat",
                                            x2 = toy_data$X3, 
                                            n2 = 3, 
                                            var_name2 = "X3",
                                            z_vec = toy_data$Tx)

# This is equivalent to pulling from the candidate library:
alt_strat <- candidates[[ 'Yhat_X3_3x3' ]]
all.equal( toy_data$strata, alt_strat )
#> [1] "'current' is not a factor"

Step 3: Draw a stratified sample

With the stratification fixed, draw the human-coded sample using generate_sample_index(). By default, the function samples proportionally within strata:

toy_data$sample <- generate_sample_index( toy_data, 100,
                                          Z = "Tx", strata = "strata",
                                          seed = 4044 )
table( toy_data$strata, toy_data$sample )
#>                   
#>                      0   1
#>   Low Yhat / X3=1   97  11
#>   Med Yhat / X3=1  101  12
#>   High Yhat / X3=1 101  12
#>   Low Yhat / X3=2   97  10
#>   Med Yhat / X3=2  102  11
#>   High Yhat / X3=2 102  11
#>   Low Yhat / X3=3  108  11
#>   Med Yhat / X3=3   95  11
#>   High Yhat / X3=3  97  11

The table shows that each of the 9 strata contributes roughly 10% of its documents to the coded sample.

To create a coding sheet for human coders:

sheet <- toy_data %>%
  filter( sample == 1 ) %>%
  dplyr::select( ID ) %>%
  mutate( Yobs = NA ) %>%
  arrange( ID )
write_csv( sheet, "coding_sheet.csv" )

Step 4: Merge coded outcomes

After coding, merge the human-coded outcomes back into the full dataset:

data( "toy_data_coded" )
head( toy_data_coded )
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>      ID   Yobs
#>   <int>  <dbl>
#> 1    57 -0.891
#> 2    59  1.41 
#> 3    64 -2.18 
#> 4    66 -3.58 
#> 5    73 -0.752
#> 6    78  0.417

full_data <- toy_data %>%
    left_join( toy_data_coded, by = "ID" )

# Verify all targeted documents were coded
table( sampled=full_data$sample, has_outcome = !is.na( full_data$Yobs ) )
#>        has_outcome
#> sampled FALSE TRUE
#>       0   807   93
#>       1    93    7

The next table summarizes surrogate bias and residual error within each stratum:

sum_stat <- full_data %>%
  group_by( strata ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_code = sum(sample),
             mean_Yhat = mean( Yhat ),
             mean_Y = mean( Yobs, na.rm=TRUE ),
             bias = mean_Yhat - mean_Y,
             err = sd( Yobs - Yhat, na.rm=TRUE ) ) %>%
  arrange( -mean_Yhat )
sum_stat
#> # A tibble: 9 × 7
#>   strata               n n_code mean_Yhat mean_Y    bias   err
#>   <fct>            <int>  <dbl>     <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 High Yhat / X3=3   108     11      5.19  3.74   1.45   1.48 
#> 2 High Yhat / X3=2   113     11      4.73  3.91   0.811  0.641
#> 3 High Yhat / X3=1   113     12      4.63  4.82  -0.183  0.421
#> 4 Med Yhat / X3=3    106     11      1.30  0.645  0.658  2.40 
#> 5 Med Yhat / X3=1    113     12      1.20  1.25  -0.0534 0.352
#> 6 Med Yhat / X3=2    113     11      1.11  0.508  0.602  1.07 
#> 7 Low Yhat / X3=1    108     11     -2.16 -2.38   0.223  0.342
#> 8 Low Yhat / X3=2    107     10     -2.18 -1.22  -0.960  1.21 
#> 9 Low Yhat / X3=3    119     11     -2.52 -0.741 -1.78   1.42

Because the stratification crosses Yhat and X3, we can plot bias and residual error across Yhat levels within each X3 group:

sum_stat_plot <- sum_stat %>%
  separate( strata, into = c("Yhat_strat", "X3_strat"), sep = " / " ) %>%
  mutate( Yhat_strat = factor( Yhat_strat,
                               levels = c( "Low Yhat", "Med Yhat", "High Yhat" ) ) ) %>%
  pivot_longer( cols = c(bias, err),
                names_to = "stat", values_to = "val" )

ggplot( sum_stat_plot, aes( Yhat_strat, val,
                            col = X3_strat, group = X3_strat ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ stat, scales = "free_y" ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 0, linetype = 2 ) +
  labs( x = "Yhat stratum", y = "Value", color = "X3 stratum" ) +
  theme_minimal()

When bias differs across strata, the stratified estimator corrects those differences within strata rather than averaging them over the full sample. The residual error panel (err) shows whether some strata have noisier surrogate predictions than others. If that heterogeneity is large, optimal allocation may be worth considering.

Step 5: Estimate the treatment effect

The est_ma_strat() function computes the stratified model-assisted estimator. It combines the full-sample surrogate predictions with within-stratum bias corrections estimated from the coded subsample:

es <- est_ma_strat( data = full_data,
                    Yobs = "Yobs",
                    Z = "Tx",
                    S = "sample",
                    strata = "strata",
                    Yhat = "Yhat" )
es
#>   est SE SEhat SEhat.full SEhat.samp S2.0 S2.1
#> 1  NA NA    NA         NA         NA   NA   NA

The main outputs are est (the ATE estimate) and SEhat (the estimated standard error). For comparison, we can also compute the SRS model-assisted estimator, which ignores the stratification:

es_srs <- est_ma_srs( data = full_data,
                       Yobs = "Yobs",
                       Z = "Tx",
                       S = "sample",
                       Yhat = "Yhat" )
es_srs
#>   est SE SEhat SEhat.full SEhat.samp S2.0 S2.1
#> 1  NA NA    NA         NA         NA   NA   NA

Because the sample was stratified, this SRS calculation is not the estimator we would use for inference. It is included only to show how the standard errors compare in this example.

Power analysis

Before collecting human-coded outcomes, it is useful to ask how much coding is needed to reach a target level of precision and how much stratification changes that calculation.

First estimate the design parameters from pilot data:

R2s <- estimate_R2( full_data, Yobs = "Yobs", Yhat = "Yhat",
                    Z = "Tx", strata = "strata" )
R2s
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   R2_strat     n     K R2_ML
#>      <dbl> <int> <int> <dbl>
#> 1 -0.00410  1000    18 0.825

Then plot MDES (minimum detectable effect size) curves as a function of the coding fraction:

target_MDES <- 0.25
pp <- plot_power_curve( nrow(full_data), mean(full_data$Tx), 1,
                        R2_ML = R2s$R2_ML, R2_strat = R2s$R2_strat )

# Plot with target MDES line
pp +
  geom_hline( yintercept = target_MDES, lty = 3 ) +
  scale_y_continuous( breaks = seq(0, 0.3, by = 0.05) ) +
  expand_limits( y = 0 )

The underlying values are stored as an attribute of the plot:

tbl <- attr( pp, "table" )
head( tbl )
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   Method         h    SE  MDES
#>   <chr>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Stratified  0.05 0.132 0.369
#> 2 Stratified  0.06 0.122 0.343
#> 3 Stratified  0.07 0.115 0.323
#> 4 Stratified  0.08 0.110 0.308
#> 5 Stratified  0.09 0.105 0.295
#> 6 Stratified  0.1  0.102 0.284

Use the table to find where each curve is closest to the target MDES:

crosses <- tbl %>%
  group_by( Method ) %>%
  filter( abs(MDES - target_MDES) == min(abs(MDES - target_MDES)) )
crosses
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#> # Groups:   Method [2]
#>   Method         h     SE  MDES
#>   <chr>      <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Stratified  0.15 0.0893 0.250
#> 2 SRS         0.15 0.0892 0.250

In this toy example, the stratified design reaches the target at about an 11% coding fraction.

The ratio of required sample sizes tells us how much stratification reduces the coding burden:

1 - crosses$h[[1]] / crosses$h[[2]]
#> [1] 0

Here, stratification reduces the required coding effort by about 27%.

  • vignette("applied_analysis") for a detailed walkthrough of evaluating and selecting from possible stratifications, including oracle vs. pre-coding comparisons and optimal allocation.

References

Mozer, Reagan, and Luke Miratrix. 2025. “More Power to You: Using Machine Learning to Augment Human Coding for More Efficient Inference in Text-Based Randomized Trials.” The Annals of Applied Statistics 19 (1): 440–64.
Mozer, Reagan, Nicole E Pashley, and Luke Miratrix. 2026. “Stratified Sampling for Model-Assisted Estimation with Surrogate Outcomes.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2602.12992.
